title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
應天府鄉試錄序
皇上臨御之二年為正德丁卯適
天下賓興賢能之歲先是禮
部臣以故事
聞
上若曰惟
天惟
===
祖宗所以眷命垂裕者實在於此
其亟行之毋忽至是應天府
臣
請官主試事而左諭德臣珪侍
讀臣清則被
命而往至則挾藝而就試者已
雲集矣提調則有府尹臣銳

punctuated:
應天府鄉試錄序

皇上臨御之二年，為正德丁卯，適天下賓興賢能之歲。先是，禮部臣以故事聞。上若曰：「惟天惟祖宗，所以眷命垂裕者，實在於此。其亟行之，毋忽！」至是，應天府臣請官主試事，而左諭德臣珪、侍讀臣清則被命而往。至則挾藝而就試者已雲集矣。提調則有府尹臣銳
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

The second year of His Majesty’s reign was the dingmao year of the Zhengde era [1507], a year when worthy and capable men throughout the realm were to be received as honored guests and recommended for office. Previously, the officials of the Ministry of Rites had submitted a report in accordance with established precedent. His Majesty spoke thus: “It is indeed upon this that Heaven and Our ancestors’ favor and mandate, and the abundant blessings they bequeath to posterity, depend. Proceed with it promptly; do not be negligent!”

At this point, the officials of Yingtian Prefecture requested the appointment of officials to preside over the examination. The Left Mentor, your servant Gui 珪, and the Reader-in-waiting, your servant Qing 清, received the command and went there. Upon their arrival, candidates bringing their literary accomplishments to the examination had already gathered like clouds. Serving as Proctor was the Prefect, your servant Rui 銳 …

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
府丞臣堂監試則有監察御
史臣昊臣郭所以戒其事於
外同考試則有學正臣巽教
諭臣翰臣思禮臣進臣德器臣孔清
訓導臣璣臣鼎臣積中所以分
其事於內小大百須罔不具
備臣等何所庸其力哉惟精
===
白一心詳校閱嚴去取而已
三試既畢如式取百三十五
人并刻其文之優者二十篇
為錄以
獻其限於式而不能盡取不能
盡刻者亦多矣錄成臣珪當
叙諸首簡竊惟
alt_text:
府丞〔臣堂〕監試則有監察御
史〔臣昊臣郭〕所以戒其事於
外同考試則有學正〔臣畢〕教
諭〔臣翰臣思禮臣進臣德器臣孔清〕
訓導〔臣璣臣鼎臣積中〕所以分
其事於内小大百須罔不具
備〔臣〕等何所庸其力哉惟精
白一心詳校閱嚴去取而已
===
三試既畢如式取百三十五
人并刻其文之優者二十篇
為錄以
獻其限於式而不能盡取不能
盡刻者亦多矣錄成〔臣珪〕當
叙諸首簡竊惟
punctuated:
府丞臣堂。監試則有監察御史臣昊、臣郭，所以戒其事於外；同考試則有學正臣巽，教諭臣翰、臣思禮、臣進、臣德器、臣孔清，訓導臣璣、臣鼎、臣積中，所以分其事於內。小大百須，罔不具備，臣等何所庸其力哉？惟精白一心，詳校閱，嚴去取而已。
三試既畢，如式取百三十五人，并刻其文之優者二十篇，為錄以獻。其限於式而不能盡取、不能盡刻者，亦多矣。錄成，臣珪當叙諸首簡，竊惟：
translation_en:
…and the Prefectural Vice Prefect, your servant Tang. Supervising the examination were the Investigating Censors, your servants Hao and Guo, who ensured diligence in its external administration. Serving as Associate Examiners were the School Instructor, your servant Xun; the Instructors, your servants Han, Sili, Jin, Deqi, and Kongqing; and the Assistant Instructors, your servants Ji, Ding, and Jizhong, who shared the work within. Everything required, great or small, was fully provided. Where, then, could we servants apply our efforts? Only in keeping our minds wholly pure, reviewing the papers carefully, and rigorously deciding which to accept and which to reject.
Once the three examination sessions were completed, we selected 135 men in accordance with the regulations and had twenty of their finest essays engraved for printing, making a record to present to the throne. Because of the prescribed limits, there were also many whom we could not select and many essays we could not print. When the record was completed, it fell to your servant Gui to write a preface on its opening leaves. I humbly reflect that…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
天既全以其所覆之天下畀我
太祖高皇帝我
高皇帝受之思所以保眷命於無
窮者惟在求賢以為助故於
建元洪武之三年即
詔行科舉以起懷才抱德之士
其略云
===
朕方與斯民共享升平之治所
慮官非其人有殃吾民盖深有
以見夫治道之要未有能易
此者
列聖相承恪遵不替得人輔治日
盛一日迨我
皇上繼之尤加之意故凡

詔行科舉以起懷才抱德之士
其略云
===
朕方與斯民共享升平之治所
慮官非其人有殃吾民盖深有
以見夫治道之要未有能易
此者
列聖相承恪遵不替得人輔治日
盛一日迨我
皇上繼之尤加之意故凡
punctuated:
天既全以其所覆之天下畀我太祖高皇帝，我高皇帝受之，思所以保眷命於無窮者，惟在求賢以為助。故於建元洪武之三年，即詔行科舉，以起懷才抱德之士。其略云：「朕方與斯民共享升平之治，所慮官非其人，有殃吾民。」盖深有以見夫治道之要，未有能易此者。
列聖相承，恪遵不替，得人輔治，日盛一日。迨我皇上繼之，尤加之意，故凡
translation_en:
Heaven had bestowed upon our Taizu, the High Emperor, the entirety of the realm beneath its canopy. Our High Emperor received it and considered how to preserve Heaven’s favor and mandate forever: this depended solely on seeking worthy men to assist him. Thus, in the third year of the Hongwu era, he issued an edict instituting the civil-service examinations to bring into service men endowed with talent and virtue. It read in part: “I am now sharing with these people the blessings of peaceful government. My concern is that officials may be unsuitable for their posts and bring calamity upon my people.” This indeed reveals a profound understanding of the essentials of governance; nothing can supersede this principle.
The successive sage emperors scrupulously adhered to this practice without abandoning it. They secured capable men to assist in governing, and flourishing rule grew day by day. When our present Emperor succeeded them, he devoted still greater attention to it. Thus, in all …

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
郊
天享
廟
耕藉
視學
開史局
御經筵
===
祖宗
列聖所必行而不可廢之禮既以
次舉行所謂求賢為助
祖宗
列聖之所慎重焉者則尤慎之重
之不敢少忽於是冗官則汰
之小大百司之不職者則罪

punctuated: 郊天、享廟、耕藉、視學、開史局、御經筵，祖宗列聖所必行而不可廢之禮，既以次舉行；所謂求賢為助，祖宗列聖之所慎重焉者，則尤慎之重之，不敢少忽。於是冗官則汰之，小大百司之不職者則罪
translation_en: …the suburban sacrifice to Heaven, offerings at the ancestral temple, ploughing the imperial field, visiting the imperial school, opening the Historiography Office, and attending the Classics Colloquium—the rites that the imperial ancestors and successive sage sovereigns invariably performed and that could not be abandoned—have now been carried out in due sequence. As for seeking worthy men to assist in government, a matter the imperial ancestors and successive sage sovereigns treated with care and gravity, His Majesty exercises still greater care and attaches still greater weight to it, daring not be the least neglectful. Thus he dismisses superfluous officials, and those throughout the offices, high and low, who fail in their duties he punishes…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之黜之其賢能過人者則超
擢而顯用之
國家閒暇文恬武嬉誠有因循
玩愒者矣至是悉惴惴供事
惟不稱厥職以負
上意是懼盖當泰亨熙洽之餘一
旦出其振迅奮厲之偉烈以
===
赫然震耀於天下而不使其
有怠廢不舉之患固宜中外
臣工丕應傒志之若是也雖
書之所稱率作興事詩之所
稱薄言震之莫不震疊亦何
以過是哉今爾諸士之出適
際其時幸以其平日之所懷

擢而顯用之
國家閒暇文恬武嬉誠有因循
玩愒者矣至是愁惴惴供事
惟不稱厥職以負
上意是懼蓋當泰亨熙洽之餘一
旦出其振迅奮厲之偉烈以
===
赫然震耀於天下而不使其
有怠廢不舉之患固宜中外
臣工丕應傒志之若是也雖
書之所稱率作興事詩之所
稱薄言震之莫不震疊亦何
以過是哉今爾諸士之出適
際其時幸以其平日之所懷
punctuated: 之，黜之；其賢能過人者，則超擢而顯用之。國家閒暇，文恬武嬉，誠有因循玩愒者矣。至是，悉惴惴供事，惟不稱厥職以負上意是懼。盖當泰亨熙洽之餘，一旦出其振迅奮厲之偉烈，以赫然震耀於天下，而不使其有怠廢不舉之患，固宜中外臣工丕應傒志之若是也。雖《書》之所稱「率作興事」，《詩》之所稱「薄言震之，莫不震疊」，亦何以過是哉？今爾諸士之出，適際其時，幸以其平日之所懷
translation_en: …them and dismiss them; those whose worth and ability surpass others he promotes beyond the usual ranks and appoints to prominent service. With the realm at peace and leisure, civil officials had grown complacent and military officers given themselves to pleasure; there were indeed those who merely followed established routines and idled away their time. Now all attend to their duties with anxious care, fearing only that they might fail to fulfil their offices and thereby disappoint the sovereign’s expectations. After a period of prosperity and harmonious rule, he has suddenly displayed the magnificent achievements of his vigorous and resolute action, striking awe throughout the realm and ensuring that no duties fall into neglect or remain unperformed. It is surely fitting that officials at court and in the provinces should respond so fully and unite their resolve [?] in this way. Even what the Book of Documents calls “leading them to undertake and advance their tasks,” and what the Book of Odes calls “he roused them with his might, and none failed to tremble,” could hardly surpass this! Now you scholars come forward at precisely this moment. We hope that what you have long cherished…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
蓄所抱負者形之乎言語文
字之間藹然德義之所呈露
曄然才美之所著見以見知
於主司以登名是錄使主司
者讀其言而可以槩得其為
人曰此蓋有德者之言其所
抱負者何如也曰此又有才
===
者之言其所懷蓄者何如也
彬彬濟濟誠無忝乎
聖詔之所云者則古人所謂實之
美者其發也不揜蓋亦庶幾
矣行將捷春官奉
大對進而與在位臣工並列於
中外以今日之所言者舉而

punctuated: 蓄所抱負者，形之乎言語文字之間，藹然德義之所呈露，曄然才美之所著見，以見知於主司，以登名是錄。使主司者讀其言，而可以槩得其為人，曰：「此蓋有德者之言，其所抱負者何如也！」曰：「此又有才者之言，其所懷蓄者何如也！」彬彬濟濟，誠無忝乎聖詔之所云者，則古人所謂「實之美者，其發也不揜」，蓋亦庶幾矣。行將捷春官，奉大對，進而與在位臣工並列於中外，以今日之所言者舉而
translation_en: …what you have stored up and the aspirations you cherish, giving them expression in speech and writing, so that your virtue and righteousness are abundantly revealed and your fine talents shine forth. Thus may you gain recognition from the presiding examiners and have your names entered in this record. Let the presiding examiners read your words and thereby gain a general understanding of your character, saying: “These are surely the words of a virtuous man—what aspirations he cherishes!” And again: “These are the words of a talented man—what riches he has stored within!” Refined and dignified, you would truly live up to the words of the imperial edict. Then you would come close to what the ancients meant when they said: “When the substance within is beautiful, its outward expression cannot be concealed.” Soon you will succeed in the examination held by the Ministry of Rites, respectfully present your answers at the Palace Examination, and advance to stand alongside the officials serving at court and in the provinces, taking what you have said today and…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
措之施為建立之間務俾斯
民得以享升平之治而不罹
其殃豈非
聖心之所致望於天下者矧諸士
為畿甸之英先天下而興尤
聖心之所厚望者哉盖
皇上求賢圖治之心即
===
祖宗垂裕之心亦即
上天眷命之心也今之中外臣工
固莫不心
皇上之心矣爾諸士顧獨不知所
以心
皇上之心以求無負哉果無負焉
則
alt_text:

其殃豈非
聖心之所致望於天下者矧諸士
為畿甸之英先天下而興尤
聖心之所厚望者哉蓋
皇上求賢圖治之心即
===
祖宗垂裕之心亦即
上天眷命之心也令之中外臣工
固莫不心
皇上之心矣爾諸士顧獨不知所
以心
皇上之心以求無負哉果無負焉
則
punctuated:
措之施為建立之間，務俾斯民得以享升平之治，而不罹其殃，豈非聖心之所致望於天下者？矧諸士為畿甸之英，先天下而興，尤聖心之所厚望者哉！盖皇上求賢圖治之心，即祖宗垂裕之心，亦即上天眷命之心也。
今之中外臣工，固莫不心皇上之心矣。爾諸士顧獨不知所以心皇上之心，以求無負哉？果無負焉，則
translation_en:
…put them into practice in your actions and accomplishments, striving to ensure that these people may enjoy peaceful and prosperous government without suffering its calamities. Is this not what His Majesty hopes for throughout the realm? How much greater, then, are his expectations of you gentlemen, the outstanding talents of the metropolitan region, who rise before the rest of the realm! For His Majesty’s desire to seek worthy men and achieve good government is precisely the desire of his imperial ancestors to bequeath enduring blessings, and likewise the intent of Heaven above in bestowing its favor and mandate.
The officials now serving at court and in the provinces surely all take His Majesty’s purposes as their own. Can you gentlemen alone fail to understand how to take His Majesty’s purposes as your own, so as not to disappoint him? If indeed you do not disappoint him, then…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
皇上必將是信是使漸以進于大
僚之列他日豈無樹芳勳揚
偉績隱然為
國名臣者否則黜罰之加如今
日亦恐或不能免矣盖
奉
天法
===
祖實
皇上今日惓惓意也臣故懇懇為
諸士道之願相與共砥厲焉
奉直大夫左春坊左諭德兼
翰林院侍講傅珪謹序
alt_text:
皇上必將是信是使漸以進于大
僚之列他日豈無樹芳勲揚
偉績隱然為
國名臣者否則黜罰之加如今
日亦恐或不能免矣盖
奉
天法
===
祖實
皇上今日惓惓意也〔臣〕故懇懇為
諸士道之願相與共砥厲焉
奉直大夫左春坊左諭德兼
翰林院侍講傅〔珪〕謹序
punctuated:
皇上必將是信是使，漸以進于大僚之列。他日豈無樹芳勳、揚偉績，隱然為國名臣者？否則黜罰之加，如今日亦恐或不能免矣。盖奉天法祖，實皇上今日惓惓意也。臣故懇懇為諸士道之，願相與共砥厲焉。
奉直大夫、左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍講傅珪謹序。
translation_en:
…His Majesty will surely trust and employ you, gradually advancing you into the ranks of high officials. In days to come, will there not be among you those who establish illustrious merit, achieve magnificent accomplishments, and become eminent ministers of the realm through their quiet authority? Otherwise, I fear that you may not escape dismissal and punishment, such as are imposed today. For revering Heaven and emulating the imperial ancestors are indeed His Majesty’s earnest concerns today. Your servant has therefore spoken earnestly of these matters to you gentlemen, hoping that we may encourage one another and strive together.
Preface respectfully composed by Fu Gui, Grand Master for Upright Service, Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy.

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
正德二年應天府鄉試
提調官
應天府府尹沈銳〔文進浙江仁和縣人己丑進士〕
中憲大夫應天府府丞李堂〔時升浙江鄞縣人丁未進士〕
考試官
奉直大夫左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍講傅珪〔邦瑞直隸清苑縣人丁未進士〕
翰林院侍讀顧清〔士廉直隸華亭縣人癸丑進士〕
同考試官
順天府通州儒學學正洪異〔大同福建龍溪縣人乙卯貢士〕
===
浙江衢州府西安縣儒學教諭羅榦〔定本江西永豐縣人辛酉貢士〕
直隸真定府無極縣儒學教諭甘思禮〔秉節廣西蒼梧縣人戊午貢士〕
四川順慶府西充縣儒學教諭趙進〔登遠湖廣漢陽縣人乙卯貢士〕
江西廣信府上饒縣儒學教諭蔡德噐〔用之浙江黄巖縣人辛酉貢士〕
山東兖州府鄒縣儒學教諭劉孔清〔濬源福建閩縣人乙卯貢士〕

Proctors

Examiners

Associate Examiners

Hong Yi, Instructor in the Confucian School of Tongzhou, Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Datong and was a native of Longxi County, Fujian. He became a tribute student (gongshi) in the yimao year.

四書

子謂韶：「盡美矣，又盡善也。」
思知人，不可以不知天。
未有仁而遺其親者也，未有義而後其君者也。

易

元者，善之長也；亨者，嘉之會也；利者，義之和也；貞者，事之幹也。君子體仁，足以長人；嘉會，足以合禮；利物，足以和義；貞固，足以幹事。
解，利西南，往得衆也。
是故君子所居而安者，易之序也；所樂而玩者，爻之辭也。
介如石焉，寧用終日？斷可識矣。

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said of the Shao music: “It is perfectly beautiful, and also perfectly good.”
To seek to understand human beings, one must understand Heaven.
Never has a benevolent person neglected his parents; never has a righteous person put his ruler last.

Book of Changes (Yijing)

The originating is the foremost of goodness; the flourishing is the gathering of excellence; the beneficial is the harmony of righteousness; the firm is the supporting framework of affairs. By embodying benevolence, the gentleman is able to lead others; by bringing excellence together, he is able to accord with ritual propriety; by benefiting things, he is able to harmonize righteousness; by remaining firm and steadfast, he is able to manage affairs.
For Deliverance, the southwest is favorable: by going there, one gains the multitude.
Thus, what the gentleman rests in contentedly is the sequence of the Changes; what he delights in and ponders is the wording of the lines.
Firm as a rock—why wait until the end of the day? His judgment can be discerned.

Book of Documents (Shujing)

I wish to hear the six pitch standards, the five notes, and the eight kinds of instrumental sound, to discern good government or neglect through the presentation and reception of words sung to the five notes. Attend to this.

德懋，懋官；功懋，懋賞。

冢宰掌邦治，統百官，均四海；司徒掌邦教，敷五典，擾兆民；宗伯掌邦禮，治神人，和上下；司馬掌邦政，統六師，平邦國；司寇掌邦禁，詰姦慝，刑暴亂；司空掌邦土，居四民，時地利。

惟文王、武王敷大德于天下，用克受殷命。

詩

淑人君子，其儀一兮！其儀一兮，心如結兮！

濟濟蹌蹌，絜爾牛羊，以往烝嘗。或剥或亨，或肆或將，祝祭于祊。祀事孔明，先祖是皇，神保是饗。孝孫有慶，報以介福，萬壽無疆。執爨踖踖，為俎孔碩；或燔或炙，君婦莫莫，為豆孔庶。為賓為客，獻酬交錯，禮儀卒度，笑語卒獲。神保是格，報以介福，萬壽攸酢。

干祿百福，子孫千億。穆穆皇皇，宜君宜王。

允也天子，降予卿士，實維阿衡，實左右商
translation_en:
Where virtue is outstanding, confer an elevated office; where achievement is outstanding, confer a generous reward.

The Minister of State directs the governance of the realm, oversees the hundred officials, and brings order throughout the four seas. The Minister of Education directs the realm’s instruction, disseminates the five teachings concerning human relationships, and brings harmony to the myriad people. The Minister of Rites directs the realm’s rituals, regulates relations between spirits and humans, and harmonizes those above and below. The Minister of War directs the realm’s military administration, commands the six armies, and pacifies the states. The Minister of Justice directs the realm’s prohibitions, investigates wickedness, and punishes violence and rebellion. The Minister of Works directs the realm’s lands, settles the four classes of people, and develops the land’s resources in accordance with the seasons.

Kings Wen and Wu spread their great virtue throughout the world and thereby succeeded in receiving the mandate formerly held by Yin.

Book of Odes

That good and noble man—how constant his deportment! How constant his deportment, his heart as firmly bound as a knot!

Dignified and moving with measured steps, purify your cattle and sheep and bring them to the winter and autumn sacrifices. Some flay, some cook; some lay out the offerings, some present them. The invocator offers sacrifice at the temple gate. The sacrificial service is most splendid: the ancestors are honored, and the ancestral spirits partake. The filial descendant receives their favor; they repay him with great blessings and boundless longevity. Those tending the cooking fires are reverently attentive; the sacrificial stands are laden with large portions. Some roast meat over the flames, some broil it. The lord’s wife is solemnly attentive; the offering vessels are exceedingly numerous. Guests and visitors receive and return the wine cups in mingled succession. Every ceremony accords with its proper measure; every laugh and word is fitting. The ancestral spirits arrive and repay them with great blessings, requiting them with long life.

Seek emoluments and a hundred blessings, with descendants in their thousands and millions. Reverent and splendid, fit to be a lord, fit to be a king.

Truly a Son of Heaven! [Heaven] sent us a high minister: he was indeed A-heng, the chief minister, who assisted Shang …

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

In winter, in the tenth month, there was no rain. 〔Second year of Duke Xi.〕 In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, there was no rain; in summer, in the fourth month, there was no rain. 〔Third year of Duke Xi.〕

In autumn, in the eighth month, the regional lords entered into a covenant at Shouzhi. The Earl of Zheng fled home without joining the covenant. 〔Both entries are from the fifth year of Duke Xi.〕 In the eighth month, on the jiaxu day, they jointly entered into a covenant at Pingqiu. The Duke did not participate in the covenant. 〔Both entries are from the thirteenth year of Duke Zhao.〕

The Viscount of Wu sent Zha on a diplomatic visit to our state. 〔Twenty-ninth year of Duke Xiang.〕

In the third month, the Duke met at Shaoling with the Viscount of Liu, the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Marquis of Wei, the Viscount of Chen, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Dun, the Viscount of Hu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, the Viscount of Xiaozhu, and Guo Xia of Qi, and they invaded Chu. In winter, in the eleventh month, on the gengwu day, the Marquis of Cai, with the Viscount of Wu, fought the men of Chu at Boju. The army of Chu was routed. 〔Both entries are from the fourth year of Duke Ding.〕

He leads the Three Dukes, the Nine Ministers, the regional lords, and the grand masters, and personally plows the imperial sacrificial field. The Son of Heaven pushes the plow three times; the Three Dukes, five times; and the ministers and regional lords, nine times. On returning, he takes up a wine cup in the principal sleeping chamber. The Three Dukes, the Nine Ministers, the regional lords, and the grand masters all attend. This is called the wine of recompense for labor.

Thus, when the gentleman rides in his carriage, he hears the sound of the luan and he bells; when he walks, he makes his jade pendants chime…

translation_en:
…what they taught them was simply the five human relationships. Yet in the Rites of Zhou, the Minister of Education (dasitu) also administered twelve forms of instruction, and at the beginning of each year publicly displayed the instructional statutes. Why was this? Was the flourishing government and admirable popular customs of that age indeed brought about by the excellence of its methods of instruction, or did they have some other source? Thereafter, among the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song, some sat upright and lectured in person, while others summoned all the learned teachers. They cannot be said to have been incapable of teaching, yet commentators considered that there had been none [?]. Some first established the Imperial University, and others first established prefectural and commandery schools. They cannot be said to have disregarded learning, yet commentators considered them late in doing so. If we consider the foundations upon which our Sagely Founder imparted instruction and the year in which he established schools, the matter becomes clear.
Today, the school system is uniform throughout the realm, and methods of instruction are the same in places near and far. Moreover, the Sagely Founder’s establishment of the school system and methods of instruction began in the Southern Capital, Nanjing; you candidates have long heard much about these matters and delighted in discussing them. Set forth fully the means by which the Sagely Founder taught, and assess them against those of the emperors and kings of antiquity. In this way, demonstrate how our Sagely Founder equaled those rulers in greatness and bequeathed abundant blessings to subsequent sage rulers, thereby providing instruction for ten thousand generations.

儒有疎爽之稱班固之作前漢書而先
儒有寥塞之語二子何修何爲而能至
punctuated:
問：自濂洛關閩諸儒出而道學明，其說布於天下，父兄以之教子弟，學校以之作人材，科目以之取士。章甫縫掖之流，非是莫之講者，不知於所謂道者，果真見其全體大用之所在而不差，而所謂學者，果諸儒之成法而不謬耶？其所講明，果可以措諸行事而不為空言耶？昔之大儒若荀况氏、揚雄氏、韓愈氏，猶不免於擇焉不精、語焉不詳之病，今之學者何談之易也！無亦其間有雷同而附和者歟？然吾觀于今，文治蔚興，賢才輩出，其間豈無遡濂洛之波、踵關閩之跡而興者？是又不可以槩論也。請著其平日之所切磋與所得於心者以對，庶有考於他日。

問：作史之難尚矣。司馬遷之作史記，而先儒有疎爽之稱；班固之作前漢書，而先儒有密塞之語。二子何修何為而能至
translation_en:
Question: Since the scholars of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min emerged and clarified the Learning of the Way, their teachings have spread throughout the realm. Fathers and elder brothers use them to instruct their sons and younger brothers; schools use them to cultivate talent; and the examination system uses them to select scholars. Among those who wear scholars’ caps and wide-sleeved robes, there are none who discuss anything else. Yet we do not know: concerning what they call the Way, have they truly perceived, without error, where its complete substance and great functioning lie? And does what they call learning indeed accord with the established methods of those scholars, without deviation? Can what they expound actually be put into practice, rather than remain empty words? Even such great Confucian scholars of the past as Xun Kuang, Yang Xiong, and Han Yu could not escape the faults of insufficient discrimination in choosing and insufficient precision in speaking. How readily scholars today speak of it! Might there not be some among them who merely echo others and join in agreement? Yet when I consider the present, civil governance flourishes and worthy talent emerges in succession. Surely among them there are those who rise by tracing the currents of Lian and Luo to their source and following in the footsteps of Guan and Min. Thus one cannot judge them all indiscriminately. Please set down in your reply what you have examined and discussed in your daily studies and what you have grasped in your own mind, so that there may be a basis for assessing you in days to come.

Question: The difficulty of writing history has long been recognized. Earlier Confucian scholars characterized Sima Qian’s Records of the Historian as loosely structured and lucid, and Ban Gu’s History of the Former Han as densely detailed and constricted. What did these two men cultivate, and what did they do, that enabled them to attain…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
是豈其天資學力有過人者歟抑家庭
之間授受有所自歟史記所載有所謂
六家之論者其要指何歸漢書所載有
所謂六子之薦者其推奬何為史記有
本紀有表有書有世家有列傳漢書有
帝紀有年表有志有列傳其篇目大畧
始終大義可得聞歟二書俱有缺畧之
處而補之者何人所補者亦有得失之
可議歟固稱遷有良史才矣然又謂其
===
論大道則先黃老而後六經叙游俠則
退處士而進姦雄述貨殖則崇埶利而
羞貧賤有所指歟范曄稱固有良史才
矣然又謂其論議常排死節否正直而
不叙殺身成仁之為美有所見歟其文
其事之評具有成說保身之道亦有一定
論諸士子讀史之時自槩於胷中久矣
豈無優劣之分歟自今有作當以何者
為法幸盡言之

===

退處士而進姦雄述貨殖則崇埶利而
羞貧賤有所指歟范曄稱固有良史才

其事之評具有成說保身之道亦有定
論諸士子讀史之時自縣於胷中久矣
豈無優劣之分歟自今有作當以何者
為法華盡言之
punctuated: 是？豈其天資學力有過人者歟？抑家庭之間授受有所自歟？《史記》所載有所謂六家之論者，其要指何歸？《漢書》所載有所謂六子之薦者，其推奬何為？《史記》有本紀，有表，有書，有世家，有列傳；《漢書》有帝紀，有年表，有志，有列傳。其篇目大畧、始終大義，可得聞歟？二書俱有缺畧之處，而補之者何人？所補者亦有得失之可議歟？固稱遷有良史才矣，然又謂其論大道則先黃老而後六經，叙游俠則退處士而進姦雄，述貨殖則崇埶利而羞貧賤，有所指歟？范曄稱固有良史才矣，然又謂其論議常排死節、否正直，而不叙殺身成仁之為美，有所見歟？其文其事之評，具有成說；保身之道，亦有一定論。諸士子讀史之時，自槩於胷中久矣，豈無優劣之分歟？自今有作，當以何者為法？幸盡言之。
translation_en:
…this level? Was it that their natural gifts and scholarly attainments surpassed those of others? Or did their learning derive from instruction transmitted within their families? In the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), there is what is called the discussion of the Six Schools: what is the essential purport of its argument? In the History of the Han (Hanshu), there is what is called the recommendation of the six men: what prompted this commendation? The Records of the Grand Historian contains Basic Annals, Tables, Treatises, Hereditary Houses, and Collected Biographies; the History of the Han contains Imperial Annals, Chronological Tables, Treatises, and Collected Biographies. May we hear an outline of their contents and the principal meanings running through them from beginning to end? Both books contain omissions: who supplied the missing portions? Do these supplements also have merits and faults that warrant discussion?

Ban Gu praised Sima Qian as possessing the talent of a fine historian. Yet he also said that, in discussing the Great Way, Sima Qian placed the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi before the Six Classics; in recounting the deeds of wandering knights, he relegated scholars who remained out of office to a lower place while advancing unscrupulous men of power; and in describing the acquisition of wealth, he exalted power and profit while treating poverty and low station as shameful. Did these criticisms have specific targets? Fan Ye praised Ban Gu as possessing the talent of a fine historian. Yet he also said that Ban Gu’s judgments repeatedly disparaged those who died for their principles and censured the upright, while failing to recount the beauty of sacrificing one’s life to fulfill humaneness. What observations underlay this judgment?

There are established assessments of their writings and their deeds, and there is also a settled judgment concerning the way to preserve oneself. You candidates, in reading history, have surely long weighed these matters in your minds. Can you have failed to distinguish their relative merits? If one were to undertake such writing henceforth, which should one take as a model? Please set forth your views in full.

text:

勸之而使勉于為善刑罰所以懲之而
使憚于為惡二者人主之大權也然世
降風移則有非爵賞所能勸刑罰所能
懲者書之旌别淑慝禮之節惠尊名所
以輔二者之不及而施之無窮也試與
諸生論之旌别之令先儒以為仁之至

輿臨問者有兄弟同居四十餘年而改
鄉為義感里名和順者有宗族七百口
同居共爨而旌為義門者其流風何美

同取義亦異史冊所載其法甚嚴春秋

punctuated: 問：國家之馭臣下，勸與懲而已。爵賞所以勸之而使勉于為善，刑罰所以懲之而使憚于為惡，二者人主之大權也。然世降風移，則有非爵賞所能勸、刑罰所能懲者。《書》之旌别淑慝，《禮》之節惠尊名，所以輔二者之不及而施之無窮也。試與諸生論之。旌别之令，先儒以為仁之至、義之盡，又以為善善長、惡惡短。漢唐而下，嘗倣而行之矣。故有為郡守而賜金百斤、下詔稱揚者，有為刺史而被以三公之服者，有居喪哀毀而璽書降問、旌其門閭者，有九世同居而累朝旌表、乗輿臨問者，有兄弟同居四十餘年而改鄉為義感、里名和順者，有宗族七百口同居共爨而旌為義門者。其流風何美也！今可指而言之歟？節惠之典，為說不同，取義亦異。史冊所載，其法甚嚴；春秋以降，盖或爽其實矣。故有自愛謚傳而
translation_en:
Question: The state's governance of its subjects consists simply in encouragement and punishment. Ranks and rewards encourage them and induce them to strive to do good; penalties and punishments chastise them and make them shrink from doing evil. These two constitute the great powers of the ruler. Yet as the ages decline and customs change, there are those whom ranks and rewards cannot encourage and penalties and punishments cannot deter. The Book of Documents' distinction between the virtuous and the wicked, and the Book of Rites' provision for summing up a person's deeds and honoring his name, supplement what these two powers cannot accomplish and extend their effects without limit. Let us discuss this with you candidates.

Earlier Confucian scholars regarded the injunction to distinguish virtue from wickedness as the utmost expression of benevolence and the fullest realization of righteousness. They also understood it to mean extending recognition of goodness while limiting condemnation of evil. From the Han and Tang onward, this was imitated and put into practice. Thus there was a commandery governor who was granted a hundred jin of gold and commended by imperial edict; a regional inspector who was clothed in the robes of the Three Dukes; a man so wasted by grief during mourning that an imperial letter under seal was sent to inquire after him and his gateway was publicly honored; a family whose nine generations lived together, which received commendations through successive reigns and was visited by the emperor; brothers who lived together for more than forty years, on whose account their township was renamed Yigan and their village Heshun; and a lineage of seven hundred people who lived together and shared their cooking fires, which was honored as a Righteous Household. How admirable was the influence they left behind! Can you now identify these cases and discuss them?

As for the institution of summing up a person's deeds in a posthumous title, explanations differ, as do the meanings drawn from it. The standards recorded in the histories are very strict; from the Spring and Autumn period onward, however, some titles seem to have failed to accord with the facts. Thus there was one who himself cherished the transmission of a posthumous title [?] and …

蓋欲使

未有不以是為重者人時之授百穀之

punctuated:
終得令名者，有忠孝無聞而卒蒙美謚者，有謚曰文貞、中被浮言而卒不可易者，有謚為文正、中遭駁議而卒從改易者，有始謚曰肅、請益以忠而弗得者，有始謚曰文、有司建請而益以忠者。其持論何嚴也！今可舉而陳之歟？我國家旌別贈謚，具有彝典。聖天子勵精初政，動法祖宗。近者既勅有司申明黜陟，而於贈謚尤以濫予為禁，蓋欲使恩威所加，人知勸沮，以復治古之規也。諸生抱藝而来，適際斯會，有可以為新政助者，尚無訥于言。
問：農，天下之大本也。自古帝王之治天下，未有不以是為重者。人時之授，百穀之播，溝洫之力，仇餉之征，九一之耕，見於載籍者可考已。《周禮》遂人、匠人之所掌，
translation_en:
…and ultimately obtained a fine reputation. There were those whose loyalty and filial devotion were unheard of, yet who ultimately received a fine posthumous name; those given the posthumous name Wenzhen (Cultured and Upright), which, despite intervening rumors, ultimately could not be changed; those given the posthumous name Wenzheng (Cultured and Correct), which, after objections were raised, was ultimately changed; those initially named Su (Solemn), for whom a request to add Zhong (Loyal) was denied; and those initially named Wen (Cultured), to which Zhong was added at the responsible officials’ request. How exacting were the judgments in these matters! Can you now cite and explain these cases? Our dynasty has established statutes governing the bestowal of distinctions and posthumous names. Our sagely Son of Heaven applies himself diligently at the outset of his reign, modeling his every action on his ancestors. Recently he commanded the responsible officials to reaffirm the rules for demotion and promotion, expressly prohibiting indiscriminate grants of posthumous names. His intention is that, wherever imperial favor and authority reach, people should know what to strive for and what to avoid, thereby restoring the standards of ancient good government. You students have come with your scholarly attainments at this opportune moment. If you have anything that might assist the new administration, do not hesitate to speak.
Question: Agriculture is the great foundation of all under Heaven. Since antiquity, no emperor or king governing the realm has failed to attach importance to it. The announcement of the seasons for human labor, the sowing of the hundred grains, work on irrigation channels, the exaction of provisions [?], and cultivation under the system of one part in nine—all these can be examined in the written records. As for the responsibilities of the Directors of Suburban Districts and the Master Craftsmen in the Rites of Zhou…

text:
其即九一之法否歟先儒井田之說亦
有合於周禮者歟井田之壞或謂魯宣
公或謂秦商鞅孰任其咎其流之弊何
所止極歟漢初乏用上下困矣文帝何
得與成康並稱或謂能用鼂賈務農之
言不知其所言者果何謂歟武帝之初
可謂庶而富矣何至與始皇並列當時
之賢亦有以農事說者而或未盡用不
知其所說者果何指歟魏孝文之均田
===
唐太宗之世業皆留心農事者也而其
法又何以不行歟洪惟我
太祖高皇帝
天縱聰明深知稼穡其
聖政之見於養民者雖不昫昫於既往之迹而
常脗合乎帝王之道蓋嘗有
勸農之言屢播於
詔令稅田之法特著於令甲固萬世臣民所
宜遵行而佩服者也爾諸士子明習

太祖高皇帝
天縱聰明凙知稼穡其
聖政之見於養民者雖不拘拘於既往之迹而
常脗合乎帝王之道蓋嘗有

詔令稅田之法特著於令甲固萬世臣民所
宜遵行而佩服者也爾諸士子明習
punctuated: 其即九一之法否歟？先儒井田之說，亦有合於周禮者歟？井田之壞，或謂魯宣公，或謂秦商鞅，孰任其咎？其流之弊，何所止極歟？漢初乏用，上下困矣，文帝何得與成康並稱？或謂能用鼂賈務農之言，不知其所言者果何謂歟？武帝之初，可謂庶而富矣，何至與始皇並列？當時之賢，亦有以農事說者，而或未盡用，不知其所說者果何指歟？魏孝文之均田，唐太宗之世業，皆留心農事者也，而其法又何以不行歟？洪惟我太祖高皇帝，天縱聰明，深知稼穡。其聖政之見於養民者，雖不昫昫於既往之迹，而常脗合乎帝王之道。蓋嘗有勸農之言，屢播於詔令；稅田之法，特著於令甲，固萬世臣民所宜遵行而佩服者也。爾諸士子明習
translation_en:
…were these indeed the methods of the one-in-nine system? Do the earlier Confucian scholars’ explanations of the well-field system also accord with the Rites of Zhou? Some attribute the destruction of the well-field system to Duke Xuan of Lu, others to Shang Yang of Qin: who bears the blame? To what extremes did the resulting abuses extend? At the beginning of the Han, resources were insufficient, and both rulers and subjects suffered hardship. How, then, did Emperor Wen come to be praised alongside Kings Cheng and Kang of Zhou? Some say that he was able to put into practice the advice of Chao Cuo and Jia Yi on promoting agriculture. What, precisely, did their advice mean? At the beginning of Emperor Wu’s reign, the people could be described as numerous and prosperous. How did he come to be ranked alongside the First Emperor of Qin? Among the worthy men of that time, some also offered advice concerning agriculture, yet their recommendations were perhaps not fully adopted. What, precisely, did they propose? Emperor Xiaowen of Wei’s equal-field system and Emperor Taizong of Tang’s hereditary landholdings both reflected concern for agriculture. Why, then, did these systems fail to remain in operation?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed by Heaven with intelligence and discernment, profoundly understood sowing and reaping. His sagely governance, as manifested in nourishing the people, did not meticulously follow [?] the precedents of the past, yet constantly accorded with the Way of the ancient emperors and kings. His exhortations to promote agriculture were repeatedly promulgated in imperial edicts, and his provisions for taxing farmland were expressly set down in the statutes. These are assuredly things that subjects and officials throughout all generations ought to observe, cherish, and uphold. You examination candidates are thoroughly versed in…

translation_en:
First Session
Four Books

The Master said of the Shao music: “It is perfectly beautiful, and also perfectly good.”
Wu Shi

Comment by Associate Examiner Liao, Assistant Instructor: Among those who addressed this topic in the examination, many failed to appreciate fully the words “beautiful” and “good.” This essay is clear in its reasoning, and its language is graceful and fluent. It should be recorded as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Hong, Instructor: Its explanation of how the sage’s music is perfectly beautiful and perfectly good leaves scarcely anything unexplored. After reading it repeatedly, I felt as though I had entered the court of Yu and heard the lingering strains of its music. Truly an excellent composition.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Reader-in-Waiting: It is not entangled in the two terms “achievement” and “virtue,” yet its meaning is complete in itself.

Comment by Examiner Fu, Left Adviser to the Heir Apparent: The prose, too, has an air of dignified ease.

The sage praised the music of Yu: its outward form was complete, and its inward feeling was complete as well. Music gives expression to achievement and virtue. Since the music of the great Shun attained such completeness in feeling and form, could anything surpass it? The Master commended and praised it; profound indeed was the impression it made upon him.

Whenever a dynasty arises, it must have music of its own. From Fuxi and Huangdi onward, there had been many creators of music; yet how magnificent was Shun’s Shao! Its foundations were laid when his reputation first reached the ruler and he succeeded to the throne; its forms became fully complete when governance was settled and his achievements accomplished. The mouth organs, great bells, and qin and se zithers brought the harmony of musical tones to its utmost perfection, and the hearts of those who heard them…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
融干戚羽旄有以備物采之華而觀之者忘倦
歌九德而間九功雝雝乎鳳鳥之和鳴也而聲
孰尚之舞九韶而協九奏蹌蹌乎百獸之率舞
也而容孰尚之謂之盡美信乎其文之備而無
以復加矣然又豈知其盡善乎蓋其聲之美不
止于音律之和也而咸寧之化實洋溢乎其中
其容之美不止乎物采之華也而至德之光實
交暢于四表揄揚詠歎依稀乎文明濬哲之風
音有盡而意無窮也俯仰周旋想像乎揖遜雍
===
===
容之狀心悅之而口不能言也謂之盡善則美
之中又有實焉而非徒以其文矣韶之為樂其
盛也一至此哉嗟夫唐虞之運中天地而興者
也前乎此者有所未至後乎此者有所不及舜
以大聖之德興于其間而地平天成萬世永賴
其治功又如此宜乎其制作之盛曠古而無倫
也夫子於此既極稱之而異時樂則韶舞又實
欲見諸行事則聖人之情可見矣然則後之居
制作之任者烏可以不考于斯

punctuated:
融。干戚羽旄，有以備物采之華，而觀之者忘倦。歌九德而間九功，雝雝乎鳳鳥之和鳴也，而聲孰尚之？舞九韶而協九奏，蹌蹌乎百獸之率舞也，而容孰尚之？謂之盡美，信乎其文之備而無以復加矣。然又豈知其盡善乎？蓋其聲之美，不止于音律之和也，而咸寧之化實洋溢乎其中；其容之美，不止乎物采之華也，而至德之光實交暢于四表。揄揚詠歎，依稀乎文明濬哲之風，音有盡而意無窮也；俯仰周旋，想像乎揖遜雍容之狀，心悅之而口不能言也。謂之盡善，則美之中又有實焉，而非徒以其文矣。韶之為樂，其盛也一至此哉！

嗟夫！唐虞之運，中天地而興者也。前乎此者有所未至，後乎此者有所不及。舜以大聖之德興于其間，而地平天成，萬世永賴，其治功又如此。宜乎其制作之盛，曠古而無倫也。夫子於此既極稱之，而異時「樂則韶舞」，又實欲見諸行事，則聖人之情可見矣。然則後之居制作之任者，烏可以不考于斯？
translation_en:
…are harmonized. Shields and battle-axes, feathers and yak-tail standards fully display the splendor of the ceremonial objects, and those who watch forget their weariness. They sing of the nine virtues, interspersing songs of the nine achievements: harmonious as phoenixes calling together—what sound could surpass this? They dance the nine movements of the Shao in accord with its nine musical sequences: stately as the hundred beasts all joining in the dance—what spectacle could surpass this? To call it perfectly beautiful is truly to acknowledge that its outward form is complete and admits of no further addition. Yet how does this alone reveal its perfect goodness? The beauty of its sound does not stop at harmonious pitches: the transforming influence that brings peace to all truly overflows within it. The beauty of its appearance does not stop at the splendor of its ceremonial objects: the radiance of supreme virtue truly spreads unhindered to the four outer limits. In its praise and chanting, one faintly perceives the spirit of cultural brilliance and profound wisdom; the sounds end, but their meaning is inexhaustible. In its bows, rises, turns, and movements, one envisions the gracious bearing of ritual deference and yielding the throne; the heart delights in it, but the mouth cannot express that delight. To call it perfectly good means that within its beauty there is also substance, and that it does not consist merely in outward form. How could the splendor of the Shao music have reached such heights!

Ah! The age of Tang and Yu arose at the midpoint of the history of Heaven and Earth. Those before it had not yet attained its heights; those after it fell short. Shun arose in that age with the virtue of a great sage: the earth was brought into order and Heaven’s work accomplished, and ten thousand generations would forever benefit. Such were his achievements in government. It is fitting that the splendor of his institutions and compositions should have been without equal throughout antiquity. The Master praised this music in the highest terms, and on another occasion said, “As for music, use the Shao dance.” He truly wished to see it put into practice; thus we can discern the sage’s feelings. How, then, could those in later ages charged with establishing institutions and composing ceremonial music fail to examine this?

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
思知人不可以不知天
蔡昂
同考試官教諭甘批說理明而遣辭順風簷
之下而有是作平日造詣可知矣高薦何忝
同考試官教諭羅批士子講知人處多涉上
文而知天處又發揮不透此篇隨題生意而理亦完足
可以式矣
考試官侍讀顧批講知人知天甚明白
考試官左諭德傅批說理之文發揮至此亦佳矣
===
人之品類固君子所欲知理之自出尤君子所
當知夫親親由於尊賢君子固欲知夫人也然
其理皆出于天又烏可以不知也哉昔夫子推
脩身之要以告哀公及此謂夫人君之脩身固
本於親親之仁而欲親親又必由尊賢之義君
子於此寧不思所以知人乎思知夫人蓋必籌
度於應接之間而鑒別之惟精不使以賢為不
肖而失其所宗也審察於羣衆之中而采擇之
惟謹不使以不肖為賢而昧於所從也夫思知

人之品類，固君子所欲知；理之自出，尤君子所當知。夫親親由於尊賢，君子固欲知夫人也；然其理皆出于天，又烏可以不知也哉？昔夫子推脩身之要以告哀公，及此，謂夫人君之脩身，固本於親親之仁，而欲親親，又必由尊賢之義。君子於此，寧不思所以知人乎？思知夫人，蓋必籌度於應接之間，而鑒別之惟精，不使以賢為不肖而失其所宗也；審察於羣衆之中，而采擇之惟謹，不使以不肖為賢而昧於所從也。夫思知
translation_en:
“If one seeks to understand people, one cannot fail to understand Heaven.”
Cai Ang

Comment by Associate Examiner Gan, Instructor: “His explanation of principle is clear, and his phrasing flows smoothly. That he could produce such a work beneath the windswept eaves of the examination hall reveals the attainments of his everyday study. He fully deserves a high recommendation!”

Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor: “When candidates explain ‘understanding people,’ they often stray into the preceding text; when they reach ‘understanding Heaven,’ their exposition fails to penetrate fully. This essay develops its meaning from the topic itself, and its account of principle is complete. It may serve as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Gu, Reader-in-Waiting: “The explanation of understanding people and understanding Heaven is very clear.”

Comment by Examiner Fu, Left Mentor: “For an essay explaining principle, to develop its exposition to this point is indeed commendable.”

The kinds and qualities of people are certainly what the gentleman wishes to understand; the source from which principle proceeds is still more something he ought to understand. Showing affection for one’s kin depends upon honoring the worthy, so the gentleman certainly wishes to understand people. Yet the principles involved all proceed from Heaven: how, then, could he fail to understand it?

Formerly, when the Master explained the essentials of cultivating oneself to Duke Ai, he reached this point and said that a ruler’s self-cultivation is indeed rooted in the benevolence of affection for his kin; yet to show affection for his kin, he must also proceed through the righteousness of honoring the worthy. At this point, could the gentleman fail to consider how to understand people? In seeking to understand them, he must weigh them in the course of his dealings and distinguish their qualities with the utmost precision, lest he take the worthy for the unworthy and thus lose those whom he should esteem. He must scrutinize people within the multitude and choose among them with the utmost care, lest he take the unworthy for the worthy and be mistaken about whom to follow. Now, seeking to understand…

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人固所以為親親之助而要其理則皆出於天
也不知夫天又可哉盖惟親親之殺出於天也
有不知焉則本原不徹而所以為降殺者莫識
其所從恩或至於倒施矣窮理盡性以求至于
命也非君子所當盡心乎惟尊賢之等出於天
也有不知焉則體統不貫而所以為等級者莫
原其所自禮或至於泛加矣極深研幾以求達
於上也非君子所當致力乎夫苟能知天則尊
賢親親各得其理而身於是乎脩矣推之政事
===
亦安有不舉哉抑斯言也夫子所以荅哀公之
問政而中庸引之以明費隱也論政而至於脩
身可謂探其本矣而復推極于知天盖本原之
地實在於是不如是不足以言聖賢之學也哀
公徒能問之不能行之而明訓格言因是以垂
之萬世君子於此亦重為吾道幸而惜當世之
不逢也噫
未有仁而遺其親者也未有義而後其君
者也

身可謂探其本矣而復推極于知天蓋本原之
地實在於是不知是不足以言聖賢之學也哀
公徒能問之不能行之而明訓格言因是以垂
之萬世君子於此亦重為吾道幸而惜當世之
不逢也噫
未有仁而遺其親者也未有義而後其君
者也
punctuated:
人，固所以為親親之助，而要其理，則皆出於天也。不知夫天，又可哉？盖惟親親之殺出於天也，有不知焉，則本原不徹，而所以為降殺者，莫識其所從，恩或至於倒施矣。窮理盡性以求至于命也，非君子所當盡心乎？惟尊賢之等出於天也，有不知焉，則體統不貫，而所以為等級者，莫原其所自，禮或至於泛加矣。極深研幾以求達於上也，非君子所當致力乎？夫苟能知天，則尊賢親親各得其理，而身於是乎脩矣。推之政事，亦安有不舉哉？抑斯言也，夫子所以荅哀公之問政，而《中庸》引之以明費隱也。論政而至於脩身，可謂探其本矣，而復推極于知天，盖本原之地實在於是，不如是不足以言聖賢之學也。哀公徒能問之，不能行之，而明訓格言因是以垂之萬世。君子於此，亦重為吾道幸，而惜當世之不逢也。噫！

未有仁而遺其親者也，未有義而後其君者也。
translation_en:
…knowing people certainly helps one cherish one’s kin; yet, traced to their essentials, these principles all come from Heaven. How, then, could one fail to know Heaven? The diminishing degrees of affection for kin come from Heaven. If one does not understand this, one fails to comprehend their source and cannot recognize the basis of these gradations; affection may consequently be bestowed in an inverted order. To investigate principle fully and fulfill one’s nature, seeking thereby to arrive at an understanding of Heaven’s mandate—is this not something to which the gentleman should devote his whole heart? The degrees of honor accorded to the worthy likewise come from Heaven. If one does not understand this, one fails to grasp the coherent order and cannot trace the source of these distinctions; ritual honors may consequently be conferred indiscriminately. To fathom the depths and examine the subtlest beginnings, seeking thereby to comprehend what is above—is this not something to which the gentleman should devote his efforts? If one can know Heaven, honoring the worthy and cherishing one’s kin will each accord with their proper principles, and one’s person will thereby be cultivated. When this is extended to affairs of government, how could anything fail to be accomplished?

Moreover, these words were the Master’s answer to Duke Ai’s question about government, and the Doctrine of the Mean quotes them to illuminate the Way’s all-pervading operation and hidden subtlety. To discuss government and arrive at self-cultivation may be called probing its root. Yet the argument proceeds still further, reaching its ultimate point in knowing Heaven, because this is truly where the source lies. Without this, one cannot adequately speak of the learning of the sages and worthies. Duke Ai could only ask about it; he could not put it into practice. Yet these illuminating teachings and exemplary sayings were thereby handed down for ten thousand generations. Here the gentleman finds further cause to rejoice for our Way, while regretting that it found no receptive ruler in that age. Alas!

“Never has there been one who was benevolent yet neglected his parents; never has there been one who was righteous yet put his ruler second.”

The great worthy traced how benevolence and righteousness benefit rulers and parents, showing that a ruler ought to practice benevolence and righteousness. For the benevolent invariably love their parents, and the righteous invariably give priority to their ruler; these virtues have never been without benefit. Should a ruler, then, fail to consider how to transform and guide his people through them? When Mencius answered King Hui of Liang’s question about benefiting his state with benevolence and righteousness, he made this statement to clarify his meaning. It is as though he were saying: only when a person lacks benevolence is his original heart fettered and lost, so that he does not know whom to love; thus there may be those who neglect their parents. But in the benevolent person, the virtue of the heart is whole and the principle of love complete: there has never been such a person who neglected his parents. I know that virtue must give first place to practicing filial piety, and love must be most earnest toward □□ [?]. In attending to and supporting their parents, they adapt to every circumstance; at the coming of dawn they think of them—at the coming of dawn they cannot forget them…

If a ruler personally practices benevolence and righteousness without a heart intent on seeking profit, those below him will be transformed and will naturally love and uphold him. How could this ever fail to be beneficial? Such, broadly, is the meaning of my statement, “There are only benevolence and righteousness.”

Yet when Mengzi sought to stop King Hui from speaking of profit, it would have sufficed to instruct him in benevolence and righteousness. What King Hui called profit meant enriching the state and strengthening its armies: making profit itself the object of pursuit. What Mengzi called benefit, however, was the natural benefit that arises when benevolence and righteousness are practiced and the people turn of their own accord to the ruler. translation_en: …in his commentary on it, had already distinguished these as four virtues, and the Commentary on the Words of the Text further elucidates them. What the Judgment calls yuan, “origination,” is the beginning of the generation of things. Among the virtues of Heaven and Earth, none precedes this. Thus, among the seasons it is spring, and in human beings it is benevolence, which encompasses all goodness. This is why origination is “the chief of goodness.” Heng, “flourishing,” is the unimpeded development of generated things. When things reach this stage of growth, all are fine and beautiful. Thus, among the seasons it is summer, and in human beings it is ritual propriety, in which all beauties gather. This is why flourishing is “the convergence of excellence.” The fulfillment of the generation of things is called li, “benefit.” Each thing attains what is appropriate to it, without interfering with or harming the others. This is autumn among the seasons and righteousness in human beings: each attains harmony in its allotted place. Is benefit not “the harmony of righteousness”? The completion of the generation of things is called zhen, “constancy.” Substantial principle is fully present, sufficient in each thing wherever it resides. This is winter among the seasons and wisdom in human beings, and it suffices to provide the foundation for affairs. Is constancy not “the foundation of affairs”? Such is the completeness of Heaven’s virtue in human beings: it lacks not the slightest particle. Is embodying it and putting it into practice not the work of the gentleman? Thus, through embodying benevolence, his moral nature becomes broad and generous; all things under Heaven come within his nurturing care, and he is thereby able to lead others. By making the convergence excellent, he renders distinctions and regulations precise and clear; everything he does in daily life converges upon pure excellence, and he is thereby able to accord with ritual propriety. By making benefit impartial and extending it, he enables every affair and every thing to attain what is appropriate to it, so that their allotted places are thereby secure. Is benefiting things not sufficient to bring righteousness into harmony? By knowing what is correct and holding to it, he ensures that judgments of right as right and wrong as wrong remain firm and unchanging, so that affairs are thereby established. Is steadfast constancy not sufficient to provide the foundation for affairs? Thus Heaven’s virtue operates and accords with human beings, and human beings embody…

With the Commentary on the Words of the Text elucidating matters to this extent, how profound is the instruction it offers later generations! Broadly speaking, the ancient sages composed the Book of Changes originally only to determine good and ill fortune through divination and thereby guide the people's actions. Only when Confucius composed the Wings did moral principles begin to be used to expound the words of the classic. The Commentary on the Words of the Text for the two hexagrams Qian and Kun, moreover, deals purely with moral principles, without admixture of images and numbers. As for distinguishing origination, flourishing, benefit, and constancy as four virtues, corresponding to benevolence, ritual propriety, righteousness, and wisdom, so that all who discuss human nature in ages to come must take them as their foundation—this goes beyond merely revealing the profound meaning of the hexagrams and their lines. title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子之介既如石矣豈用終日而後知夫幾哉大
傳釋豫六二爻義如此謂夫事之已形者易見
幾之方萌者難知六二君子所以能知幾者果
何自邪盖人之處豫也多耽戀而無特立之操
故其於事也常迷惑而無識微之明今君子也
不鳴不盱獨守其道而有中立之介弗疾弗冥
自持乎正而有永貞之節石至安靜也其德之
安靜如之凝然不可動焉石至堅確也其德之
堅確如之屹乎不可轉焉是以光明發於艮止
===
之餘不必自朝至暮而動之細微者斷可知矣
思慮明於安定之後不必自辰至酉而吉之先
見者斷可識矣諂上瀆下之幾莫不察之於先
若蓍之索隱也何終日之用乎微彰柔剛之幾
莫不辨之於早若龜之前知也何終日之俟乎
由是觀之則知見幾非難守德為難守之既堅
又何患幾之難識哉抑論之天下之理未有誠
而不明者六二君子以如石之介而有不終日
之知固其宜也子思嘗曰至誠之道可以前知

punctuated: 子之介既如石矣，豈用終日而後知夫幾哉？大傳釋豫六二爻義如此。謂夫事之已形者易見，幾之方萌者難知。六二君子所以能知幾者，果何自邪？盖人之處豫也，多耽戀而無特立之操，故其於事也，常迷惑而無識微之明。今君子也，不鳴不盱，獨守其道而有中立之介；弗疾弗冥，自持乎正而有永貞之節。石至安靜也，其德之安靜如之，凝然不可動焉；石至堅確也，其德之堅確如之，屹乎不可轉焉。是以光明發於艮止之餘，不必自朝至暮，而動之細微者斷可知矣；思慮明於安定之後，不必自辰至酉，而吉之先見者斷可識矣。諂上瀆下之幾，莫不察之於先，若蓍之索隱也，何終日之用乎？微彰柔剛之幾，莫不辨之於早，若龜之前知也，何終日之俟乎？由是觀之，則知見幾非難，守德為難。守之既堅，又何患幾之難識哉？抑論之，天下之理，未有誠而不明者。六二君子以如石之介，而有不終日之知，固其宜也。子思嘗曰：「至誠之道，可以前知。」
translation_en: …the gentleman’s integrity is already like a rock; why would he need a whole day before recognizing the first stirrings of change? Such is the Great Commentary’s explanation of the meaning of the second, yin line of the hexagram Yu (Enthusiasm). Events that have already taken shape are easy to see, but the first stirrings just beginning to emerge are difficult to recognize. What, then, enables the gentleman of the second, yin line to recognize them? People amid enjoyment often become engrossed in their pleasures and lack the resolve to stand independently. Thus, in dealing with events, they are often confused and lack the discernment to recognize what is subtle. This gentleman, however, neither proclaims his enjoyment nor gazes upward in expectation. He alone keeps to his Way, possessing the integrity to stand firm in the mean. Neither afflicted nor benighted, he holds himself to what is correct and possesses enduring constancy. A rock is supremely calm and still; his virtue is likewise calm and still, settled and immovable. A rock is supremely firm and solid; his virtue is likewise firm and solid, standing fast and unshakable. Thus, illumination emerges from the stillness expressed by Gen (Keeping Still): without waiting from morning until evening, he can assuredly recognize the subtlest beginnings of movement. His thoughts become clear after he has attained settled composure: without waiting from the hour of chen until the hour of you, he can assuredly recognize the earliest signs of good fortune. He invariably detects beforehand the first stirrings of flattery toward superiors and disrespect toward inferiors, just as yarrow stalks uncover what is hidden. What need has he of a whole day? He invariably distinguishes early the incipient tendencies of the subtle and the manifest, the yielding and the firm, just as the divinatory tortoise foreknows events. Why should he wait a whole day? Viewed in this light, recognizing the first stirrings is not difficult; maintaining one’s virtue is difficult. Once one maintains it firmly, why worry that those stirrings will be hard to recognize? To discuss this further, among the principles of the world there is no instance of sincerity without illumination. That the gentleman of the second, yin line, with his rocklike integrity, should possess understanding that requires less than a whole day is entirely fitting. Zisi once said: “The Way of utmost sincerity permits foreknowledge.” …

禹者如此臣鄰之義豈不益見其為重哉嗟夫
punctuated: 而命大臣，其任之也重矣。昔帝舜責大禹以臣鄰之義，而釋之及此，謂夫：「天下之政，本出於朝廷，而聲音之道，實通乎政事。予於汝而有所屬焉。彼六律以節五聲，而政之得失於是乎形也，予欲盡聞之，以察吾治之成與未成。五聲被於八音，而政之善否於是乎徵也，予欲兼聽之，以察吾功之著與未著。朝廷之制作，協於五音而可為法程也，出而布之，使作樂者有所本焉。里巷之歌謡，比於五聲而可觀民風也，采而納之，使審音者有所據焉。凡此皆所以考吾之治也，然豈能一一而自為之哉？亦惟禹也，竭耳力之至聰，為朕躬之司聽。精以察之，而識其始終條理之全；審以求之，而測其聲氣感通之妙。聽之而其聲和以順歟？則政之治可知，當相與慎之，而保其終焉，而予之聞惟汝之聞矣。聽之而其聲乖以逆歟？則政之忽可知，當相與更之，而圖其始焉，而汝之聽即予之聽矣。」吁！舜之所以責禹者如此，臣鄰之義，豈不益見其為重哉？嗟夫！
translation_en:
…and charges a high minister with this task: weighty indeed is the responsibility he entrusts to him. In former times, Emperor Shun charged the Great Yu with the duty of a minister as his close associate, and his explanation extended to this matter. His meaning was: “The governance of the realm originates in the court, while the principles of musical sound are intimately connected with affairs of government. I therefore have a charge to entrust to you. The six pitch standards regulate the five notes, and through them the successes and failures of government become manifest. I wish to hear them all, to examine whether my governance has attained its proper fruition. The five notes are expressed through the eight classes of instruments, and through them the goodness or failings of government are revealed. I wish to listen to them together, to examine whether my achievements have become manifest. Those compositions of the court that accord with the five notes and can serve as standards should be issued and disseminated, so that those who make music have something on which to base their work. The songs of the lanes and alleys that accord with the five notes and allow the customs of the people to be observed should be collected and brought in, so that those who scrutinize music have evidence on which to rely.

“All these are means of examining my governance. Yet how could I undertake each of them myself? It is for you, Yu, to exercise your hearing to its utmost acuity and act as the listener for my own person. Examine the music with precision, and apprehend the entirety of its ordered structure from beginning to end; investigate it carefully, and fathom the subtle ways in which sound and vital force resonate and communicate. When you listen, are its sounds harmonious and well ordered? Then we may know that government is well administered. Together we should attend to it carefully and preserve its good conclusion; what I hear will be what you hear. When you listen, are its sounds discordant and unruly? Then we may know that government is neglected. Together we should reform it and plan a new beginning; what you hear will be what I hear.”

“Ah!” Such was the charge Shun laid upon Yu. Does this not make still clearer the weight of a minister’s duty as the ruler’s close associate? Alas! …

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有虞之時何時也百獸舞而鳳凰儀萬國寧而
蠻夷服泰和盛治蓋亘古而一見者也而舜之
命禹惓惓以審音察政為言乃若其政之多辟
而懼於不終者聖人之心其不自滿假固如此
也即是而觀則夫致貞觀之小康而以禮樂無
關於政治者其何止天地之相遠哉噫此古治
之所以不復也
惟文王武王敷大德於天下用克受殷命
余翃

translation_en:
…What an age was the time of Yu! The hundred beasts danced and the phoenix appeared in stately grace; the myriad states were tranquil, and the Man and Yi peoples submitted. Such supreme harmony and flourishing government were surely seen but once in all antiquity. Yet when Shun charged Yu, he spoke earnestly of scrutinizing music to examine government, as though his government had many faults and he feared that it might not endure to the end. Such indeed is the sage’s refusal to become complacent or self-satisfied. Viewed in this light, how much greater than the distance between heaven and earth is the gulf separating him from one who achieved the modest prosperity of the Zhenguan era yet considered rites and music irrelevant to government! Alas! This is why the good government of antiquity has never returned.
“King Wen and King Wu spread their great virtue throughout All under Heaven, and thereby succeeded in receiving Yin’s mandate.”
Yu Hong
Comment by Associate Examiner Gan, Instructor: Whenever one writes an essay, if one’s understanding of principle is unsound, even a polished composition is not worth reading. This essay alone stands apart from the other compositions [?]; it is included here for more than its diction.
Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor: Candidates can generally discuss the difficulty of taking possession of Yin, but their treatment of the spreading of virtue mostly lacks orderly and fluent exposition. Moreover, the paired sections’ presentation places undue emphasis on moving the ruler [?], making them tiresome to read. In achieving excellence in both diction and reasoning, this essay alone is the best.
Comment by Examiner Gu, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: It expansively portrays Wen and Wu receiving the mandate, with a magnificent grandeur.
Comment by Examiner Fu, Left Admonisher: The development of the word “difficult” at the end of the essay is particularly meaningful.
Only because the former kings spread their great virtue far and wide did the great mandate finally come to them. How very difficult it is to receive the mandate! Had King Wen and King Wu not spread their great virtue throughout All under Heaven, how then …

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
何以能受殷命而有天下也哉昔康王命畢公
保釐東郊首告之以此若謂今日之化殷民也
固難而先世之受殷命也尤難獨不觀諸文武
乎惟我文王以大德而創之於前武王以大德
而成之于後是故徽柔懿恭文王之大德也有
以誕敷於天下而無遺執競維烈武王之大德
也有以徧布於天下而無外觀夫惠鮮懷保而
咸和乎萬民有德有造而譽髦乎斯士其德之
誕敷也可知散財發粟而四海為之永清惇信
===
明義而萬姓為之悅服其德之徧布也可見文
開之武承之用是有殷之大命不能舍之而他
歸父作之子述之用是有商之大統不能外之
而他往故誕膺天命以撫方夏人徒知文王之
能受殷命也而不知其大德之敷非一朝一夕
之故矣豈易得者邪崇德報功垂拱而治人徒
知武王之能承商統也而不知其大德之布非
一日二日之積矣豈易致者邪曰敷大德私恩
小惠不足言也曰於天下一家一國不足言也

一日二日之積矣豈易致者邪曰敷大德私恩
□惠不足言也曰於天下一家一國不足言也
punctuated: 何以能受殷命而有天下也哉？昔康王命畢公保釐東郊，首告之以此，若謂今日之化殷民也固難，而先世之受殷命也尤難，獨不觀諸文武乎？惟我文王以大德而創之於前，武王以大德而成之于後。是故徽柔懿恭，文王之大德也，有以誕敷於天下而無遺；執競維烈，武王之大德也，有以徧布於天下而無外。觀夫惠鮮懷保而咸和乎萬民，有德有造而譽髦乎斯士，其德之誕敷也可知；散財發粟而四海為之永清，惇信明義而萬姓為之悅服，其德之徧布也可見。文開之，武承之，用是有殷之大命不能舍之而他歸；父作之，子述之，用是有商之大統不能外之而他往。故誕膺天命，以撫方夏，人徒知文王之能受殷命也，而不知其大德之敷非一朝一夕之故矣，豈易得者邪？崇德報功，垂拱而治，人徒知武王之能承商統也，而不知其大德之布非一日二日之積矣，豈易致者邪？曰敷大德，私恩小惠不足言也；曰於天下，一家一國不足言也。
translation_en:
…how could they have received Yin’s Mandate and possessed all under Heaven? Formerly, when King Kang commanded the Duke of Bi to safeguard and govern the eastern suburbs, he began by telling him this. It was as though he were saying: transforming the people of Yin today is certainly difficult, but receiving Yin’s Mandate in former generations was more difficult still. Have you not considered Kings Wen and Wu? Our King Wen, through his great virtue, laid the foundation first; King Wu, through his great virtue, subsequently brought the undertaking to completion. Thus, goodness and gentleness, excellence and reverence were King Wen’s great virtues, which he spread far throughout all under Heaven, leaving none untouched. Unwavering strength and illustrious achievement were King Wu’s great virtues, which he spread everywhere under Heaven, leaving none outside their reach. Consider how King Wen showed kindness to the bereft and cherished and protected the people, bringing harmony to them all; how he honored and encouraged these scholars, men of virtue and accomplishment. From this we can understand how widely his virtue spread. King Wu distributed wealth and opened the grain stores, bringing lasting tranquility within the Four Seas; he upheld trustworthiness and made righteousness manifest, so that all the people gladly submitted. From this we can see how universally his virtue spread.

Wen began the undertaking, and Wu continued it: thus Yin’s great Mandate could not pass them by and devolve upon another. The father initiated it, and the son carried it forward: thus Shang’s great succession could not exclude them and go elsewhere. Accordingly, King Wen received Heaven’s Mandate in its fullness and brought peace to the lands of Xia. People know only that he was able to receive Yin’s Mandate; they do not know that the spreading of his great virtue was no matter of a single morning or evening. Could the Mandate have been easy to obtain? King Wu exalted virtue and rewarded merit, governing with his robes hanging down and his hands folded. People know only that he was able to inherit Shang’s succession; they do not know that the spreading of his great virtue was no accumulation of merely one or two days. Could this have been easy to achieve? When we say ‘spread great virtue,’ private favors and petty kindnesses do not merit mention; when we say ‘throughout all under Heaven,’ a single household or a single state does not merit mention.

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
文武得殷之難如此爾畢公之臨殷民也庸可
不念之哉抑論畢公東郊之行所當務者保釐
之政耳而康王告之必先於文武受命之難者
何邪盖凡事知其難則處之必不易故周詩曰
命之不易又曰天難忱斯皆此意也彼夏癸殷
受之所為抑豈知禹湯創業之難哉此康王所
以拳拳致望於畢公而亦因以自警也厥後畢
公果克成厥終而康王亦有潤澤生民之美其
皆不負今日之言也夫
===
詩
干禄百福子孫千億穆穆皇皇宜君宜王
陳寰

千載之下讀之令人興起

詩

陳寰

translation_en:
…Such were the difficulties Wen and Wu faced in gaining dominion over Yin. You, Duke Bi, now overseeing the people of Yin—how could you fail to bear these in mind? Yet, considering Duke Bi’s mission to the eastern suburbs, his proper concern was simply the work of safeguarding and governing the people. Why, then, did King Kang, in instructing him, begin with the difficulties Wen and Wu faced in receiving the Mandate? In any undertaking, knowing its difficulty ensures that one will not treat it lightly. Thus the Poetry of Zhou says, “The Mandate is not easily maintained,” and again, “Heaven is difficult to trust.” Both express this meaning. Judging by the conduct of Gui of Xia and Shou of Yin, did they understand the difficulties Yu and Tang faced in founding their dynasties? This is why King Kang so earnestly expressed his hopes for Duke Bi, while also taking the occasion to admonish himself. Subsequently, Duke Bi indeed brought his work to a successful conclusion, and King Kang likewise won praise for benefiting the people. Surely both lived up to the words spoken that day!

Book of Poetry
“Seeking emoluments and a hundred blessings, with descendants in countless numbers. Reverent and resplendent, fit to be a lord, fit to be a king.”
Chen Huan

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Assistant Instructor: “Your explanation of what the ducal impersonator of the deceased intended in replying to the ruler on that occasion is exceptionally apt. You must be thoroughly versed in the Classic of Poetry. How could recommending you bring any discredit?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: “The poet’s unhurried expression of loyalty and love comes through beyond the words themselves. The other compositions in this examination fall far short of this one.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: “Across a thousand years, you bring to life the love that a minister of Zhou felt for his ruler. Reading this stirs and inspires the reader.”

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍讀顧批詳雅有味
考試官左諭德傅批用字造語有斟酌非苟作者
詩人頌王者得於天者盛而備故衍其後者多
而賢夫子孫之多賢人君之盛福也詩人以是
而頌王者其忠愛何深哉假樂之詩公尸答鳧
鷖而作及此謂夫吾王以顯德而宜夫民人固
無心於干祿也然上天眷吾王而降以百福不
待其有所求焉髙麗九重位已極矣而所以培
植之者方深撫有萬方業已厚矣而所以敷佑
===
之者方篤洪休繁祉畢萃于王躬凡人之望於
天者無一之弗備焉茀祿純嘏駢臻于五位凡
天之厚乎人者無一之弗有焉然此孰從而見
之彼嗣胤不昌王之祚薄矣今也慶衍岐邠而
宗英為之日茂秀鍾豐鎬而支庶為之日蕃麟
趾振振由千而至於萬也爪瓞緜緜由萬而至
於億也而何其多也哉繼承弗類王之祿微矣
今言其敬歟則穆穆然威儀之肅整言其美歟
則皇皇然體貌之端莊胙茅土而典藩維宜乎

植之者方深撫有萬方業已厚矣而所以敷佑
===
之者方篤洪休繁祉畢萃于王躬凡人之望於
天者無一之弗備焉弗祿純嘏駢臻于五位凡
天之厚乎人者無一之弗有焉然此孰從而見
之彼嗣襱不昌王之祚薄矣今也慶衍岐邠而
宗英爲之日茂秀鍾豐鎬而支庶爲之日蕃麟
趾振振由千而至於萬也瓜瓞緜緜由萬而至
於億也而何其多也哉繼承弗類王之祿微矣
今言其敬歟則穆穆然威儀之爾整言其美歟
則皇皇然體貌之端莊胙茅土而典藩維宜乎
punctuated:
考試官侍讀顧批：詳雅有味。
考試官左諭德傅批：用字造語有斟酌，非苟作者。
詩人頌王者得於天者盛而備，故衍其後者多而賢。夫子孫之多賢，人君之盛福也。詩人以是而頌王者，其忠愛何深哉！假樂之詩，公尸答鳧鷖而作。及此，謂夫吾王以顯德而宜夫民人，固無心於干祿也。然上天眷吾王而降以百福，不待其有所求焉。髙麗九重，位已極矣，而所以培植之者方深；撫有萬方，業已厚矣，而所以敷佑之者方篤。洪休繁祉，畢萃于王躬，凡人之望於天者，無一之弗備焉；茀祿純嘏，駢臻于五位，凡天之厚乎人者，無一之弗有焉。然此孰從而見之？彼嗣胤不昌，王之祚薄矣。今也慶衍岐邠，而宗英為之日茂；秀鍾豐鎬，而支庶為之日蕃。麟趾振振，由千而至於萬也；爪瓞緜緜，由萬而至於億也。而何其多也哉！繼承弗類，王之祿微矣。今言其敬歟，則穆穆然威儀之肅整；言其美歟，則皇皇然體貌之端莊。胙茅土而典藩維，宜乎
translation_en:
Examiner Gu, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Thorough, elegant, and full of savor.”
Examiner Fu, Left Exhorter of Virtue, comments: “The choice of words and construction of phrases show deliberation; this is no careless composition.”
The poet praises the king for receiving abundant and complete blessings from Heaven, so that his descendants are numerous and worthy. Numerous and worthy descendants are a ruler’s greatest blessing. How profound is the poet’s loyal affection in praising the king on this account! The poem ‘Jia Le’ (Admirable Happiness) was composed as the ritual impersonator of the ancestors’ response to ‘Fu Yi’ (Wild Ducks and Gulls). At this point, it says that our king, through his manifest virtue, acts fittingly toward the people and certainly has no thought of seeking blessings. Yet Heaven cherishes our king and sends down a hundred blessings without waiting for him to ask. Exalted amid the palace’s ninefold precincts, he has already reached the highest station, yet Heaven’s nurture of him grows ever deeper. Possessing and pacifying the myriad regions, he has already established a substantial dominion, yet Heaven’s protection grows ever more generous. Great favor and manifold blessings all gather upon the king’s person: nothing that people hope to receive from Heaven is lacking. Great good fortune and mighty blessings arrive together at the ‘five positions’ [?]: nothing with which Heaven enriches humankind is absent.
But how can this be seen? If his descendants did not flourish, the king’s good fortune would be meager. Now, however, blessings spread from Qi and Bin, and the outstanding members of the royal lineage flourish daily; excellence gathers at Feng and Hao, and the collateral branches multiply daily. Like the qilin’s noble offspring, they increase from thousands to tens of thousands; like an unbroken succession of gourds [?], they increase from tens of thousands to hundreds of millions. How numerous they are! If his successors failed to resemble their forebears in virtue, the king’s blessings would be slight. Now, speaking of their reverence, their bearing is solemnly dignified and disciplined; speaking of their excellence, their appearance is splendidly upright and stately. Invested with grants of thatch and soil, they preside over the realm’s protective fiefs; fitting indeed …

title: 正德二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
其爲君也緝熈明而宰方夏宜乎其爲王也而
何其賢也哉凡此皆人情所深願而不可必得
者而吾王悉有之天之降福尚有加於此與公
尸以是而答其君意亦至矣大抵富貴尊榮一
身之福也子孫多賢萬世之福也周之盛時武
穆文昭布列中外畢原豐郇之屬無非賢者而
其不見於載籍者尚多矣盖文武之盛德其及
於後者如是也假樂之詩雖主於稱願而一時
屬籍之盛實於此見之屏翰維持歷歲八百要
===
亦非偶然也讀是詩者尚無以爲誇
允也天子降于卿士實維阿衡實左右商
王

其爲君也；緝熈明而宰方夏，宜乎其爲王也。而何其賢也哉！凡此皆人情所深願而不可必得者，而吾王悉有之。天之降福，尚有加於此與？公尸以是而答其君，意亦至矣。大抵富貴尊榮，一身之福也；子孫多賢，萬世之福也。周之盛時，武穆文昭，布列中外，畢、原、豐、郇之屬，無非賢者，而其不見於載籍者尚多矣。盖文武之盛德，其及於後者如是也。《假樂》之詩雖主於稱願，而一時屬籍之盛，實於此見之。屏翰維持，歷歲八百，要亦非偶然也。讀是詩者，尚無以爲誇。
允也天子，降于卿士，實維阿衡，實左右商王。
梅鶚
同考試官訓導黄批：連日閱卷，類以配享爲主，而歸重伊尹，有戾本㫖。此作獨能頌美成湯，其於得尹而有天下之意，發明詳盡，足破衆惑。
同考試官教諭蔡批：題本正大，塲中作者多務牽合之說。惟此作深得本㫖，脫去舊格，其於嗣世君
translation_en:
…his being a lord; continuing in radiant enlightenment and governing the central lands, he is indeed fit to be king. How worthy they are! All these are things that human hearts profoundly desire but cannot be certain of obtaining, yet our king possesses them all. Could Heaven bestow any greater blessing than this? With these words the ancestral impersonator responds to his lord, expressing his sentiments to the fullest. Wealth, high rank, honor, and glory are blessings for one lifetime; numerous worthy descendants are blessings for ten thousand generations. In Zhou’s flourishing age, the descendants of King Wu in the mu line and of King Wen in the zhao line were arrayed throughout the court and the realm. Those of Bi, Yuan, Feng, and Xun were all worthy, and many more went unrecorded in the written histories. Such was the reach of the abundant virtue of Kings Wen and Wu into later generations. Although the poem “Jia Le” (“Felicitous Joy”) chiefly expresses praise and good wishes, it also reveals the flourishing state of the royal lineage at that time. That its defenders sustained the dynasty for eight hundred years was surely no accident. Let readers of this poem not regard its words as exaggeration.
“Truly a Son of Heaven! There was sent down to him a high minister: this was Aheng, who supported the king of Shang.”
Mei E.
Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Assistant Instructor: In reading examination scripts over the past several days, I have found that most center on sharing in the ancestral sacrifices and place the emphasis on Yi Yin, contrary to the passage’s original purport. This composition alone succeeds in praising Cheng Tang. It explains fully and in detail the idea that he gained possession of All-under-Heaven by obtaining Yi Yin’s services, and is sufficient to dispel the confusion of the others.
Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: The topic is inherently upright and grand, but most candidates in the examination hall have pursued strained interpretations. This composition alone grasps the original purport deeply and breaks free of established formulas. In its treatment of rulers of succeeding generations…

text:

同考試官教諭趙批摹寫明良胥慶之象宛
然在目

商人頌聖祖為興王之君得聖臣為興王之佐
蓋王業之興不偶然也有商王業既衰而復振
者豈非以成湯大聖得伊尹之所致乎此宜為
祫祭之詩也□□人之意若謂當商室中衰之餘
===
正夏業將傾之日我祖湯也聖敬日躋而九圍
之法式以具勇智天錫而萬邦之表正以成天
心眷之人心歸之允矣其昊天之子也三櫱畏
之兆民懷之展矣其天下之君也既有是興王
之君自得夫興王之佐於是乎有卿士曰伊尹
有焉不先時而出也出焉適當乎其時蓋天實
降之而豈人力之所及乎不後時而出也出焉
適逢乎其會是天實賜之而豈人謀之所致乎
湯既得夫尹矣於是尊而任之而號其官曰阿

商人頌聖祖為興王之君，得聖臣為興王之佐。
蓋王業之興不偶然也。有商王業既衰而復振者，豈非以成湯大聖得伊尹之所致乎？此宜為祫祭之詩也。□□人之意若謂：當商室中衰之餘，正夏業將傾之日，我祖湯也，聖敬日躋，而九圍之法式以具；勇智天錫，而萬邦之表正以成。天心眷之，人心歸之，允矣其昊天之子也；三櫱畏之，兆民懷之，展矣其天下之君也。既有是興王之君，自得夫興王之佐。於是乎有卿士曰伊尹，有焉。不先時而出也，出焉適當乎其時，蓋天實降之，而豈人力之所及乎？不後時而出也，出焉適逢乎其會，是天實賜之，而豈人謀之所致乎？湯既得夫尹矣，於是尊而任之，而號其官曰阿
translation_en:
…the circumstances in which ruler and minister encountered one another, and the proper ordering of the joint ancestral sacrifice in later generations: neither is left untreated. This answer deserves to be singled out and presented.
Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor, comments: The depiction of an enlightened ruler and worthy minister rejoicing together stands vividly before one's eyes.
Examiner Gu, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: It captures the literary style of the Hymns of Shang.
Examiner Fu, Left Admonisher, comments: Its explanation of how the A-heng assisted the ruler is beyond the reach of the other papers.
The people of Shang praised their sage ancestor as the ruler who brought the dynasty to ascendancy and who obtained a sage minister to assist that rise.
The rise of royal rule is surely no accident. Was not the revival of Shang's royal enterprise after its decline brought about by the great sage Cheng Tang obtaining Yi Yin's service? This fittingly became a poem for the joint ancestral sacrifice. The intention of the [□□] person [?] seems to have been to say: After the house of Shang had suffered decline, precisely when Xia's enterprise was about to collapse, our ancestor Tang daily advanced in sagacity and reverence, thereby becoming a complete model for the nine regions. Heaven bestowed courage and wisdom upon him, making him the exemplar and guide of the myriad states. Heaven's heart favored him, and the people's hearts turned to him: truly, he was the son of August Heaven. The three wicked powers feared him, and the multitudes cherished him: indeed, he was the ruler of all under Heaven. With such a ruler to bring the dynasty to ascendancy, naturally there came a minister to assist that rise. Thus there appeared a high minister named Yi Yin. He did not emerge before his time; his emergence came at precisely the fitting moment. Heaven itself had sent him down—how could human strength have accomplished this? He did not emerge after his time; his emergence coincided precisely with the occasion. Heaven itself had bestowed him—how could human planning have brought this about? Once Tang had obtained Yin, he honored him and entrusted him with responsibility, giving his office the title A…

text:
衡政之可否以之為倚任也事之輕重資之以
取平也秩崇望尊凡百司庶府咸屬其統理焉
尹既相夫湯矣於是以身任之而盡其職於天
子或左焉而翊贊其謨謀也或右焉而匡救其
闕失也任大責重凡大綱小紀悉歸於總理焉
所以敷政優優者在是所以敷奏其勇者在是
此其救民於塗炭之中伐夏於昏亂之後而天
下所由歸也歟詩人於宗廟之祭本其事而歌
之其意深矣抑序以此為大禘之詩為其所及
===
者遠也說者謂大禘不及羣廟之主而此詩及
之其為祫祭之詩無疑矣一詩之中於王業之
興必推其始生之祖而於其成也必及其佐命
之臣成湯之事又特反覆之而不厭美德告功
始終有序輕重有倫商詩義古而文詳此亦其
一也當時季札觀樂聞歌頌則曰其至矣哉見
大濩之舞則又以聖人之弘賛之札固博物君
子也彼謂商頌為宋人所作者奚足以知此
春秋

punctuated:
衡，政之可否，以之為倚任也；事之輕重，資之以取平也。秩崇望尊，凡百司庶府，咸屬其統理焉。尹既相夫湯矣，於是以身任之，而盡其職於天子。或左焉，而翊贊其謨謀也；或右焉，而匡救其闕失也。任大責重，凡大綱小紀，悉歸於總理焉。所以敷政優優者在是，所以敷奏其勇者在是。此其救民於塗炭之中，伐夏於昏亂之後，而天下所由歸也歟！詩人於宗廟之祭，本其事而歌之，其意深矣。抑序以此為大禘之詩，為其所及者遠也。說者謂大禘不及羣廟之主，而此詩及之，其為祫祭之詩無疑矣。一詩之中，於王業之興，必推其始生之祖；而於其成也，必及其佐命之臣。成湯之事，又特反覆之而不厭。美德告功，始終有序，輕重有倫。商詩義古而文詳，此亦其一也。當時季札觀樂，聞歌頌，則曰：「其至矣哉！」見大濩之舞，則又以聖人之弘賛之。札固博物君子也。彼謂商頌為宋人所作者，奚足以知此？

春秋
translation_en:
…Heng, the “Balancer”: in deciding whether policies were acceptable, Tang relied upon him; in weighing the relative importance of affairs, Tang drew upon him to achieve a proper balance. His rank was exalted and his standing revered; all the offices and bureaus came under his direction. Once Yi Yin became Tang’s minister, he personally shouldered this charge and fully discharged his duties toward the Son of Heaven. At his left, he assisted and furthered his plans; at his right, he corrected his shortcomings and remedied his errors. His duties were great and his responsibilities weighty: both the broad principles and the finer rules of government came under his overall management. This was what enabled Tang to administer government with ample ease, and what enabled him to display his valor. Was this not how he rescued the people from utter misery, attacked Xia after its descent into darkness and disorder, and won the allegiance of all under Heaven? At the sacrifices in the ancestral temple, the poet based his song upon these deeds. His meaning was profound indeed.

Yet the Preface identifies this as a poem for the great di sacrifice because it reaches so far back into the past. Commentators say that the great di sacrifice did not include the spirit tablets of all the ancestral temples, whereas this poem does include them. There can therefore be no doubt that it is a poem for the combined ancestral sacrifice, the xia. Within this single poem, the rise of the royal enterprise is necessarily traced back to the founding ancestor of the lineage, while its completion necessarily embraces the minister who assisted in fulfilling the heavenly mandate. The deeds of Cheng Tang, moreover, receive repeated attention without weariness. In praising virtue and proclaiming achievement, the poem maintains an orderly sequence from beginning to end and gives due proportion to matters of greater and lesser importance. The poems of Shang are ancient in meaning and detailed in expression; this is one example.

When Ji Zha witnessed the musical performances, on hearing the Hymns sung he said, “How consummate they are!” When he saw the dance of the Great Deliverance (Da Huo), he further praised it for the sage’s magnanimity. Ji Zha was certainly a gentleman of broad learning. How could those who claim that the Hymns of Shang were composed by people of Song be capable of understanding this?

Duke Xi's diligence in worrying over the lack of rain exemplified the way to rule a state and cherish its people as one's children. How fitting that the Spring and Autumn Annals should record it once each season!
Now, food depends upon grain, and grain depends upon rain. Why, early in Duke Xi of Lu's reign, did the absence of rain last so long, extending through the three seasons of winter, spring, and summer, and hindering the three tasks of storing, plowing, and tending the crops? Judging by ordinary sentiments, who would not say: “If Heaven's moisture does not descend, the various grains will not grow; it would be acceptable even to leave this unrecorded. The Spring and Autumn Annals considers that ensuring sufficient resources and loving the people had long characterized Duke Xi's benevolent government. translation_en:
…month there was no rain: this too was recorded. The wording is lengthy and is not abridged, thereby revealing his earnest concern for rain; it repeats itself without wearying, thereby expressing his solicitude for the people. Had he been lax in government and failed to make the people's troubles his own, the record would have gathered the successive seasons into a single entry to mark his negligence, as in the second year of Duke Wen. Why, then, such detail? Had he neglected administrative affairs and failed to attend to the state's concerns, the record would have combined the seasons into one entry to document his indolence, as in the tenth and thirteenth years of Duke Wen. Why, then, such fullness? Thus Duke Xi worried about the drought as each season passed, and the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded each circumstance as it arose. Would not later rulers who met Heaven-sent calamities without fear, and saw the people's suffering without compassion, find a warning here? Far-reaching indeed was the sage's intention in leaving this teaching to posterity!
Alas! At Sanglin, Tang reproached himself on six counts: such was his concern over the lack of rain. Before he had finished speaking, heavy rain fell over a thousand li. Confronted by calamity, King Xuan appealed to Heaven in “The Milky Way”: such was his concern over the lack of rain. In the end, the people rejoiced that his kingly influence was again at work. Duke Xi's concern over the lack of rain was like this; the rain in the sixth month, recorded below, was likewise its result. On this basis, Duke Xi's solicitude for the people could aspire to that of King Xuan and Tang of old. Moreover, his promotion of instruction, celebrated in “The Waters of the Pan,” and his filial piety, celebrated in “The Secluded Temple,” were qualities that the other feudal lords of the Spring and Autumn period could scarcely approach. There is no doubt that he deserves to be counted a worthy ruler of Lu. Yet construction at the South Gate exhausted the people's strength: this inevitably left a blemish on white jade. What a pity!
“The Viscount of Wu sent Zha to pay a formal visit.” Twenty-ninth year of Duke Xiang.
Zhang Nan.

His reproaches against Ji Zha are so stern that, were Zha to return to life, he could hardly fail to acknowledge their justice in his heart.
Examiner Gu, a Reader-in-waiting, comments: The language is stern and the reasoning correct. The meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals is found scarcely anywhere but in this essay.
Examiner Fu, the Left Mentor of the Heir Apparent, comments: Nothing could better express the intention of the Spring and Autumn Annals in demanding perfection of the worthy.
A worthy man declined his position and thereby brought about disorder; the Spring and Autumn Annals used his visit to convey censure: this is the point [?]. Ji Zha could not disclaim responsibility for his state’s calamity; and in recording the dispatch of Zha, the Spring and Autumn Annals could not excuse him on account of his worthiness. Consider those times: the age was in decline and the Way had grown faint; acts of violence arose on every side. The Three Bonds had collapsed and the Nine Norms were corrupted; human desires ran unchecked and heavenly principle was extinguished. At such a time, Ji Zha declined the position of ruler of Wu: four times it was offered, and he would not accept it. He went to his fief at Yanling and, once departed, never looked back. By inspiring integrity in the greedy, he greatly benefited his age; by inspiring deference in the contentious, he contributed much to moral teaching. When he came on his diplomatic visit, the Spring and Autumn Annals might properly have recorded his designation as a ruler’s son. Why, then, did it record his personal name to censure him?
To have him accept the charge and secure the altars of soil and grain was the intention of his father and elder brothers; yet Zha opposed it. To contend for the throne and assassinate King Liao was the rebellion of Ziguang; yet Zha paved the way for it.
